title: Reliable Workflow Orchestration System
subtitle: Orchestrate a days-long approval, payment, email and three internal updates so each business effect lands exactly once, state stays visible and failed steps are compensated.
author: By Sourav Banerjee

practice_prompts.label: Finish line, waits and authority
practice_prompts.hint: Which answers about done, reversibility, wait length and provider keys change the design?

practice_prompts.label: Control plane, data plane and history
practice_prompts.hint: Trace order o-123 from start request to audit summary.

practice_prompts.label: Crash after payment and the other drills
practice_prompts.hint: Detect, contain, recover and prevent for each failure mode.

practice_prompts.label: Gates, metrics and owners
practice_prompts.hint: What must be proven before a second workflow?

rubric: I defined exactly once as the business effect, not message delivery, and named payment as the irreversible step.
I made durable history the only owner of progress and explained intent-before, completion-after.
I gave each side effect its own idempotency key and a stored receipt.
I kept capped backoff with jitter separate from compensation such as a refund.
I modelled the seven-day approval as a durable timer and signal state.
I named fail-closed, degrade, queue and human paths and partitioned lanes by tenant and dependency.
I pinned running instances to their definition version.
I gated rollout on replay determinism and crash recovery before operator visibility and migration.

editorial_review.evidence: 16 November 2026: read all 46 captured sections (about 19,000 words) of the workflow-orchestration source and wrote the casebook from scratch. The brief opens on the six-system process and the irreversible payment, defines workflow, activity, side effect, business-level exactly once, idempotency key, compensation, saga and durable history before use, and adds an o-123 example taken from the source's own code and tests. Tutorial parts 1-4, 6 and 7 became walkthrough steps 1-8; part 5's records, code and tests, the retry formula, the four trade-offs and the coverage-notes gap essays moved to deep dives, with source section numbers replaced by links. Bullet-list source material was rewritten as connected prose, and list-shaped data (question tree, must/should/could, scorecard, phases, risk register, 50-minute plan) became tables. All three code blocks and all 14 figure pairs are kept beside their explanations; of the ten source tables, seven are reproduced, the two blank worksheet templates became prompts with authored worked answers, and the old sections table became reading guidance. Additions are labelled: an illustrative backoff schedule, the o-123 traces, two authored worksheet answers, an implementation trace, and caveats that the test fixtures are undefined and the no-double-charge sketch does not prove durability. Repeated sentences (the history/receipt rule, retry-storm partitioning, the outcome line) were consolidated where they repeat. No source item was omitted.

visual_review.evidence: Desktop (1280) and phone (390) screenshots show the title, five-section nav, progress rail and the never-charge-twice brief with its definitions list, o-123 trace and the core-idea figure at phone width. All 14 placed source figures were screenshotted in the built page with disclosures open and read: core loop, stress-point decision, control/data-plane topology, happy-path sequence with retry and compensate alt blocks, crash-after-payment overlay, five drills (payment crash, email/CRM, seven-day approval, definition version, API timeout with circuit breaker), four-phase rollout with owners, saga flowchart with pay:/crm:/mail:/refund: keys, model-answer architecture and 50-minute timeline. Each sits directly after the prose it illustrates, and node and branch labels match the prose; the payment-crash caption was rewritten to match that figure's transient/terminal branches.
